items.prompt: A product catalog is read far more often than it changes. Which cache pattern preserves the database as the source of truth?
constraints: The catalog database remains authoritative.
Cache misses are acceptable.
Updates must define invalidation or freshness behavior.

options.text: Use cache-aside: read the cache first, load misses from the authoritative store, populate the cache, and invalidate or expire entries after writes.
Write catalog data only to the cache and treat eviction as a normal database replacement.
Cache every value forever so catalog updates never need coordination.
Read from any cached item without checking its key, tenant, or version because catalogs are public.

feedback.Reason: Cache-aside reduces repeated reads while retaining a durable authoritative store and explicit freshness behavior.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: The application controls cache misses and writes, so the cache can be rebuilt after eviction or failure.
Details.scenarioApplication: A catalog write invalidates or versions the affected entry, and a miss reloads the current item from the database.
Details.errorCorrection: Cache-only data is lost on eviction, infinite TTL returns stale catalog data, and unscoped reads can return incorrect objects.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: The cache adds consistency and invalidation complexity, which is justified by measured read load or latency.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Eviction or cache failure would lose the only catalog copy.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Infinite retention makes updates and corrections invisible.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Cache keys must preserve object identity and any tenant or version boundary.

items.prompt: An item is updated in the database but users continue seeing the previous value from cache. Which control is required?
constraints: The cache can outlive the write.
The product has a freshness objective.
The database write and cache behavior must be coordinated.

options.text: Invalidate or update the affected cache entry after a successful authoritative write, and use a bounded TTL as a recovery limit.
Increase the cache TTL because older values are less expensive to store.
Write the cache before the database and report success if only the cache accepts the value.
Disable database writes so the cache and source cannot diverge.

feedback.Reason: Cache freshness requires an explicit write-through or invalidation contract tied to authoritative write success.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Invalidation removes stale data and TTL bounds the maximum stale interval if an invalidation is missed.
Details.scenarioApplication: The service does not report a successful business write until the source write has committed and cache handling is defined.
Details.errorCorrection: Longer TTL worsens staleness, cache-first success can lose authoritative data, and disabling writes is not a valid consistency strategy.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Synchronous invalidation adds latency and failure handling; asynchronous invalidation adds an explicit stale window.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: A longer TTL increases the stale-data window.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: A cache write is not durable authority and can succeed while the database write fails.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Removing writes avoids divergence by removing the business function, not by solving it.

items.prompt: A popular item expires and thousands of requests fetch it from the database at once. Which pattern reduces a cache stampede?
constraints: The item is safe to share among readers.
The origin has finite read capacity.
A small bounded freshness variation is acceptable.

options.text: Use request coalescing or a single-flight lock, staggered expiration or jitter, and a bounded stale or refresh strategy that protects the origin.
Set all items to expire at the same second so refresh behavior is deterministic.
Disable cache and let every request perform a database read.
Retry every database read immediately until it succeeds, regardless of origin load.

feedback.Reason: Stampede protection coordinates misses and spreads refresh work rather than allowing every caller to hit the source.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: A lock or single-flight path lets one request refresh while others wait or receive acceptable stale data; jitter avoids synchronized expiry.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team measures origin concurrency and sets a maximum refresh time and stale policy appropriate to the content.
Details.errorCorrection: Synchronized expiry causes the spike, disabling cache increases load, and immediate retries amplify an origin bottleneck.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Stale serving trades freshness for origin protection and must be explicit to the product.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Every request becoming a miss maximizes origin load.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Unbounded retries turn a read spike into a larger overload.

items.prompt: A news homepage can serve content up to two minutes old during an origin incident. Which cache policy aligns with that objective?
constraints: The freshness window is explicit.
Availability during short origin failures is valuable.
Users must not receive content older than the agreed bound without an explicit state.

options.text: Set a TTL and stale-serving or refresh policy that keeps content within the two-minute objective, and expose an explicit unavailable state after the bound.
Serve stale content forever because news freshness is subjective.
Disable caching so the homepage always depends on the origin during an incident.
Change the timestamp displayed to users so old content appears current.

feedback.Reason: Stale caching is safe only when its freshness bound and degraded behavior match the product contract.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: TTL and stale-on-error behavior can preserve a bounded old response while origin recovery occurs.
Details.scenarioApplication: The page reports its content time and switches to a visible unavailable or reduced mode when the bound expires.
Details.errorCorrection: Forever-stale data violates the objective, no cache increases origin dependency, and changing timestamps misrepresents data.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A bounded stale window improves availability but requires accurate metadata and monitoring of age.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Unbounded staleness violates a two-minute freshness requirement.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Origin-only delivery removes the stated availability benefit during origin failure.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Changing timestamps hides an accuracy problem rather than solving it.

items.prompt: One product key receives most catalog traffic and saturates a cache node. Which response should be evaluated?
constraints: The key is read-heavy.
The value can be replicated or reconstructed.
Correctness must be preserved across copies.

options.text: Use application-level replication or key spreading for the hot read, while preserving one authoritative source and measuring cache-node distribution.
Put every request for the hot key on one node because a single key must have one cache location.
Disable all caching for the hot key and direct the traffic to the already-saturated database.
Create random values for the hot item so the cache has no hot key, even though readers need the real product.

feedback.Reason: A hot read key can be spread across cache capacity when the source and invalidation contract remain authoritative.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Replicated or salted read keys distribute requests, while writes update or invalidate all relevant representations.
Details.scenarioApplication: The application reads equivalent copies, tracks hit and node load, and tests update propagation and eviction behavior.
Details.errorCorrection: One node preserves the hot spot, database fallback worsens load, and fake values break correctness.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Replication increases memory and invalidation work, so it should be justified by measured skew.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: One cache location preserves the saturation problem.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Removing cache sends more load to the saturated authoritative store.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: A cache optimization cannot change the business value into random data.

items.prompt: A relational workload has many read-only queries and the primary's write latency is rising. What is a candidate read-scaling pattern?
constraints: Queries can tolerate replica lag.
Writes must remain on the primary.
The application can route read traffic separately.

options.text: Evaluate RDS read replicas for eligible read traffic, with explicit lag monitoring, routing, and a primary-only path for writes.
Send writes to every read replica because replication makes all nodes independent writers automatically.
Use a cache as the only durable relational source so replicas are unnecessary.
Add application servers without changing database read routing because compute instances execute database queries locally.

feedback.Reason: Read replicas can offload eligible reads while preserving a primary write authority and an explicit lag contract.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: RDS read replicas receive replicated data and can serve read-only connections; the application or routing layer chooses the endpoint.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team sends stale-tolerant reads to replicas, monitors lag and errors, and keeps transactions and writes on the primary.
Details.errorCorrection: Replicas are not automatically independent writers, caches are not relational authority, and application scale does not reduce database reads.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Replica lag, connection capacity, replication cost, and failover behavior must match the read objective.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Read replicas do not become independent multi-writer databases merely through replication.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: A cache lacks the relational durability and transaction contract of the source.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: More application instances can increase database reads unless routing changes.

items.prompt: A user's write must be visible immediately in the next read, but general catalog reads can be eventually consistent. Which routing rule is appropriate?
constraints: The primary has the newest committed write.
Replicas can lag.
The application can identify read-after-write requests.

options.text: Route read-after-write or transactionally sensitive requests to the primary, and route only stale-tolerant reads to replicas with monitored lag.
Send all reads to the replica with the lowest CPU regardless of replication lag.
Hide replica lag from the application so every read path appears equivalent.
Write to the replica first and let replication make the primary current later.

feedback.Reason: Replica selection must follow the consistency contract, not just resource utilization.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: The primary provides the strongest read-after-write guarantee while replicas provide scale for reads that accept lag.
Details.scenarioApplication: The service tracks the request's consistency need or session token and chooses the endpoint accordingly.
Details.errorCorrection: Low CPU does not mean current data, hiding lag violates the product contract, and replica-first writes reverse authority.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Primary routing may reduce read scale for sensitive paths, so the application should classify reads deliberately.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: A lightly loaded replica can still have significant data lag.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: The application must know or enforce the freshness contract.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: The primary remains the relational write authority in this pattern.

items.prompt: A DynamoDB workload is read-heavy and needs microsecond-to-millisecond read acceleration with the application's access pattern unchanged. Which service should be evaluated?
constraints: DynamoDB remains authoritative.
The workload can tolerate the cache's consistency model.
The read pattern is compatible with the accelerator.

options.text: Evaluate DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) as a managed read-through cache, while validating consistency, availability, invalidation, and cost for the workload.
Replace DynamoDB with S3 because objects provide the same key-value read API and cache behavior.
Use an RDS read replica because every DynamoDB operation can be replicated into a relational engine automatically.
Cache all writes in a browser so the DynamoDB table receives no authoritative updates.

feedback.Reason: DAX is purpose-built to accelerate DynamoDB reads while DynamoDB remains the durable source.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: DAX provides a managed in-memory cache integrated with DynamoDB APIs and has documented consistency and availability behavior.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team tests hit rate, stale-read tolerance, cluster failure, warm-up, and cost before placing DAX in the read path.
Details.errorCorrection: S3 is object storage, RDS replicas do not automatically replicate DynamoDB operations, and browser writes cannot be authoritative.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: DAX adds a cluster and a consistency boundary, so workloads needing strongly current reads may not fit every cached path.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: S3 does not provide the same low-latency key-value API or item semantics.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: DynamoDB and RDS have different data models and replication paths.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Client cache state is untrusted and cannot replace the authoritative write path.

items.prompt: A missing product item causes expensive database queries on every request. Which cache behavior may protect the source?
constraints: The item-not-found result is safe to cache briefly.
A newly created item must become visible within a defined bound.
The source remains authoritative.

options.text: Cache a negative result with a short TTL and invalidate it when the item is created, while preserving an authoritative lookup path.
Cache not-found forever because missing objects cannot become present later.
Return a fake product for every miss so the database receives no further queries.
Disable all cache behavior because only successful values can be cached safely.

feedback.Reason: Negative caching can protect an origin against repeated misses if its TTL and invalidation reflect object creation.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: The application stores a short-lived not-found representation and removes it when the authoritative state changes.
Details.scenarioApplication: A newly created product invalidates the negative entry so readers do not wait for the full negative TTL.
Details.errorCorrection: Forever-negative results hide new data, fake products corrupt correctness, and disabling all caching ignores a valid protection pattern.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A short TTL trades source load for a bounded delay in discovering newly created data.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: An item can be created later, so permanent negative caching is incorrect.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Fake data is not an acceptable cache miss response.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Negative caching is a legitimate pattern when its freshness and invalidation are explicit.

items.prompt: The cache cluster becomes unavailable while the database remains healthy but has limited read capacity. What should the application do?
constraints: The cache is an acceleration layer.
The source has finite capacity.
The application must remain correct during cache failure.

options.text: Fall back to the authoritative store with bounded concurrency, protection or degraded behavior, and alarms for cache loss and source saturation.
Treat cached values as authoritative even though the cache cannot be read and return guessed values on misses.
Retry cache connections without limit on every request and also query the database repeatedly.
Disable database reads and return successful empty results until the cache returns.

feedback.Reason: A cache failure should preserve correctness while protecting the source from a thundering fallback storm.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: The source remains authoritative, but concurrency limits, admission control, and explicit degraded behavior prevent a cache outage from becoming database exhaustion.
Details.scenarioApplication: The service may serve a reduced experience or queue work while operators restore cache capacity and monitor source health.
Details.errorCorrection: Unavailable cache values cannot be guessed safely, unbounded retries amplify the outage, and fake empty success corrupts responses.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Fallback may increase latency or reduce availability, so cache redundancy and source headroom should be designed as well.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: A missing cache value is not evidence of the correct business value.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Unbounded retries consume application and source capacity.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Empty successful data is a silent correctness failure.

items.prompt: A cache reaches memory capacity and evicts frequently requested entries, causing poor hit rate. What should be measured before adding nodes?
constraints: The workload has a finite cache budget.
Evictions may be caused by item size, TTL, or workload skew.
The authoritative source must remain safe under misses.

options.text: Measure hit rate, eviction rate, item size, key popularity, TTL, and source load, then choose policy, data-shape, or capacity changes based on the bottleneck.
Increase TTL for every item without checking whether stale data or memory pressure is acceptable.
Delete the authoritative database so cache misses cannot occur.
Add random keys to increase the apparent cache hit rate without changing data access.

feedback.Reason: Cache capacity decisions need workload evidence because memory pressure, skew, and freshness can have different causes.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Metrics reveal whether evictions come from oversized values, ineffective TTL, hot-key skew, or insufficient cache capacity.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team changes serialization, TTL, partitioning, or nodes and validates source load and correctness after the change.
Details.errorCorrection: Longer TTL can worsen memory and staleness, removing the source is unsafe, and random keys do not improve useful hit rate.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: More cache capacity costs money and does not solve a poor key or invalidation model.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Longer TTL can consume memory and serve stale values.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: The cache cannot replace the durable authoritative store.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Synthetic keys do not serve real requests or improve useful cache efficiency.

items.prompt: A read replica is saturated by one expensive report query while transactional reads remain latency-sensitive. Which architecture change is appropriate?
constraints: The report has a different workload profile.
Transactional reads should not compete with analytics.
The source of truth remains transactional.

options.text: Separate the reporting path using an appropriate read copy or analytical service, and keep transactional reads on capacity sized for their service objective.
Add more transactional application instances so the expensive report query finishes faster on the replica.
Run the report on the primary because the primary is always the most scalable read target.
Cancel transactional reads during reporting so the replica can use all capacity for one query.

feedback.Reason: Different read workloads should not share a capacity boundary when one analytical query can impair transactional objectives.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: A reporting copy or purpose-built analytical path isolates query shape, refresh, and scaling behavior from the transactional store.
Details.scenarioApplication: The report accepts its freshness contract while customer reads retain predictable capacity and monitoring.
Details.errorCorrection: Application scale does not speed a database query, the primary is not automatically a report engine, and canceling customer reads violates availability.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A read copy adds replication and freshness cost but protects the critical transactional path.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: More callers do not make an expensive database query faster.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: The primary is the write authority and may be the most sensitive path.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Protecting one query by disabling customer reads is not a valid service design.

items.prompt: Which data should generally receive the shortest cache TTL?
constraints: The data varies frequently.
The business impact of stale values is high.
The origin can absorb the resulting reads or has another read-scaling path.

options.text: Data whose correctness or freshness changes frequently and whose stale representation could cause a material business or security error.
Immutable versioned assets that never change after publication.
Public documentation whose source changes once per quarter and has a visible version.
A static logo whose object name changes whenever the bytes change.

feedback.Reason: TTL should reflect the freshness and correctness risk of the representation, not a universal cache preference.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Short TTL or no shared caching limits stale exposure for volatile or sensitive data, while immutable objects can use long TTLs.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team maps each response class to a freshness objective and confirms origin capacity for misses.
Details.errorCorrection: Immutable or versioned content does not need frequent revalidation, and visible slow-changing documentation has a longer safe window.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Shorter TTL improves freshness but increases origin work and latency on misses.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Immutable versioned objects can be cached for long periods safely.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Slow-changing public content can use a longer TTL when its versioning and freshness are clear.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Changing the object name makes the new version a new cache key.

items.prompt: A shared cache serves multiple tenants and the key is only the record ID. What should be corrected?
constraints: Record IDs can repeat between tenants.
Cache reads can bypass the database authorization check.
Tenant identity is available from authenticated context.

options.text: Include tenant scope in the cache key and enforce authorization before or with the read so a hit cannot return another tenant's value.
Trust the record ID alone because the cache cluster is shared only by the application.
Use a public cache key and depend on obscurity of tenant identifiers.
Disable tenant authorization on cache hits because the database would have checked it on misses.

feedback.Reason: Cache keys and authorization must preserve the same tenant boundary as the authoritative read path.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Namespacing prevents collisions, but the application must still derive and verify tenant context because a cache hit may skip the source.
Details.scenarioApplication: The service constructs keys from trusted identity and rejects a request whose tenant does not own the record.
Details.errorCorrection: A shared cluster does not make IDs globally unique, obscurity is not authorization, and cache hits still need an access decision.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Tenant-aware keys can affect memory distribution and hot-key behavior, which should be measured.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Shared infrastructure does not guarantee globally unique record IDs or access scope.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Guess-resistant keys are not an authorization control.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: A cache hit is precisely the path that can bypass a database authorization check.

items.prompt: A cache was added but database load and p99 latency did not improve. Which evidence should be reviewed?
constraints: The cache may be missing or returning small values.
The source and cache have separate latency and capacity metrics.
The architecture should not retain an ineffective layer without evidence.

options.text: Measure hit and miss rate, cache latency, eviction, key distribution, source query shape, stale or error responses, and end-to-end p99 before changing the design.
Add more cache nodes immediately because any poor cache result means capacity is the only problem.
Increase TTL indefinitely because longer retention always increases hit rate enough to solve latency.
Remove source metrics because a cache should make database behavior irrelevant.

feedback.Reason: Cache effectiveness depends on hit behavior, key design, item size, source query cost, and end-to-end latency, not node count alone.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Observability identifies whether requests miss, evict, serialize, query inefficiently, or spend time elsewhere in the path.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team can simplify or tune the canonical cache path based on measured benefit and correctness.
Details.errorCorrection: More nodes do not fix a poor key or low hit rate, infinite TTL can create staleness, and source metrics remain essential.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Instrumentation costs resources but prevents retaining a complex layer with no service benefit.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Capacity is only one possible cause of low benefit.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Infinite TTL can increase stale data and memory pressure without fixing misses.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: The source remains part of the fallback and correctness path and must be observed.

items.prompt: A deployment replaces a cache cluster and causes an origin read spike. Which release behavior reduces the risk?
constraints: The origin has finite capacity.
Cache contents can be rebuilt.
The application can warm popular or critical keys gradually.

options.text: Warm or prime critical entries gradually, limit fallback concurrency, monitor origin load, and roll out cache changes with a bounded recovery path.
Replace all cache capacity at once and let every request rebuild the cache concurrently.
Disable origin protection during warm-up so the cache fills as quickly as possible.
Return cached values from the old cluster after it has been deleted.

feedback.Reason: Cache replacement is an origin-capacity event and should be staged like any other dependency change.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Warm-up and bounded misses prevent a cold cache from producing an uncontrolled source burst.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team measures cache readiness and source concurrency and keeps an explicit unavailable or degraded state if the source cannot absorb all misses.
Details.errorCorrection: Concurrent rebuild creates a stampede, removing protection worsens load, and deleted cache data cannot be read reliably.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Warming consumes capacity before traffic arrives, so the key set and rate should be selected from evidence.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Replacing all capacity at once maximizes misses and source pressure.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Origin protection is most important while the cache is cold.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Deleted cache capacity cannot serve a dependable recovery path.

items.prompt: A checkout price must reflect the latest committed promotion, while a product description may be minutes old. Which design principle applies?
constraints: Price affects a financial decision.
Description freshness has a lower business risk.
The application can classify reads by consistency requirement.

options.text: Use a stricter primary or authoritative read for price and a separately bounded cache policy for descriptions, with the consistency contract visible in the service API.
Use one long TTL for both values because a shared page should have one universal freshness rule.
Cache the price forever because promotions change less often than descriptions.
Read the description from the primary and the price from any replica because text is more important than a financial value.

feedback.Reason: Different data elements have different correctness and freshness requirements and should not inherit one undifferentiated cache rule.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: The service can choose authoritative or replicated paths per read contract and use TTL or invalidation appropriate to each representation.
Details.scenarioApplication: Checkout uses current pricing while catalog pages accept bounded description staleness and expose no misleading mixed state.
Details.errorCorrection: One TTL ignores risk differences, permanent price caching is unsafe, and replica selection should follow business consistency rather than text versus number.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Multiple consistency paths add API and testing complexity but protect important business invariants.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: A universal freshness rule can be too weak for price or too expensive for all content.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Promotion changes and financial decisions make indefinite price caching unsafe.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: The chosen path should reflect the price consistency objective, not the data type label.

items.prompt: Which evidence supports keeping a cache or read-scaling layer in the canonical architecture?
constraints: The layer adds cost and consistency behavior.
The source remains authoritative.
The service objective includes measurable latency, throughput, or origin-load goals.

options.text: Show measured hit rate or read offload, end-to-end latency improvement, safe freshness and authorization behavior, failure fallback, and cost against the service objective.
Keep the layer because every production architecture should contain a cache regardless of workload evidence.
Hide stale or missing values so dashboards show only cache hits and the layer appears successful.
Remove source monitoring because a cache makes the authoritative store operationally irrelevant.

feedback.Reason: A cache or read replica earns its place by measurable benefit with an explicit correctness and failure contract.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Hit ratio, source offload, latency, consistency, authorization, fallback, and cost show whether the extra boundary improves the workload.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team keeps, simplifies, or removes the layer based on evidence and does not hide stale or unavailable states.
Details.errorCorrection: A cache is not universal, hidden misses do not prove success, and the source remains required for authority and fallback.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Caching can materially improve a read-heavy workload but adds invalidation, warm-up, capacity, and failure behavior.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: A cache without workload benefit adds cost and failure surface.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Hiding misses and stale responses prevents honest evaluation.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: The authoritative store remains part of the correctness and recovery path.
